strengths: The paper offers a clear and practically intuitive framework that organizes diffusion inference-time methods into local refinement and global tree search. The BFS-resampling, BFS-pruning, and adaptive DFS variants are described with useful pseudocode and compute-aware motivation.

The empirical scope is unusually broad, spanning long-horizon maze planning, nine D4RL locomotion tasks, compositional text-to-image generation, and ImageNet conditional generation. Results generally indicate that verifier-guided search can outperform naive best-of-N sampling at comparable neural-function-evaluation budgets.

Several practical choices are valuable, including using separate hyperparameter-search and evaluation seeds in offline RL, studying adaptive computation in DFS, and using separate guidance and selection verifiers to reduce classifier exploitation.
weaknesses: The claimed theoretical grounding is incomplete. Proposition 1 effectively assumes the conclusion when converting the guidance update into Langevin dynamics: merely taking a_t, b_t, and c_t to zero does not yield the stated unit-coefficient SDE unless their limiting ratios are controlled. The target exponent lambda is not derived, and the assertion that the scaled mean-guidance vector field is the gradient of some annealed verifier is not generally justified because such a field need not be conservative. Consequently, equivalence to sampling from p_0(x)f(x)^lambda is not established.

Novelty is limited relative to the cited literature. Local search largely reinterprets existing recurrent training-free guidance as Langevin MCMC, while resampling/pruning are close to particle filtering, sequential Monte Carlo, beam search, and recent diffusion inference-time search methods. The paper does not empirically compare against the most relevant recent approaches, including Feynman-Kac steering and Ma et al.'s diffusion search methods.

The image-generation evaluation is too narrow for the broad claims. ImageNet experiments use only two classes and 256 samples per class, making per-class FID noisy and biased; no uncertainty is reported. In CompBench, the same task-specific models act as search verifiers and benchmark evaluators, creating evaluation leakage and leaving unclear whether improvements transfer to independent metrics or human judgments.

The planning evidence lacks strong task-level baselines such as conventional collision-aware planners or recent diffusion motion-planning methods. Results use only about 40 samples per setting without confidence intervals, while the verifier has access to the ground-truth maze geometry. It is therefore difficult to assess significance or practical competitiveness beyond improving this particular diffusion sampler.

The offline-RL result is competitive but not clearly superior: its average score is slightly below QGPO and Diffusion-QL, and several individual tasks regress substantially. There are no controlled local-only, best-of-N-only, and compute-matched ablations across these tasks, nor wall-clock or verifier-cost comparisons. Extensive per-task tuning further weakens the training-free efficiency claim.

Reproducibility is insufficient. The project-page link is blank, code is not supplied, several final search thresholds and temperatures are omitted, and the reported grid-search and total tuning costs are not fully specified. BFS also uses independent rounding of offspring counts, so its population and compute budget are not guaranteed to remain fixed; this implementation detail is neither analyzed nor normalized clearly in the comparisons.

strengths: The empirical scope is unusually broad: the paper applies a common inference-time framework to maze planning, offline reinforcement learning, compositional text-to-image generation, and class-conditional image generation.
The local/global decomposition is intuitive, and the BFS/DFS presentations make the proposed inference procedures relatively easy to understand and implement.
The paper evaluates performance as a function of inference compute and discusses practically relevant issues such as adaptive compute allocation and verifier hacking.
The appendices provide pseudocode, implementation settings, and task-specific hyperparameters; the offline-RL evaluation also separates hyperparameter-search and evaluation seeds.
weaknesses: The central theoretical claim in Proposition 1 is not established as written. An update with drift a_t score(q_t) + c_t grad log(f_t) and noise coefficient b_t represents Langevin dynamics for the claimed composition only under specific relative-scaling conditions. The proof merely sends all three coefficients to zero, then replaces the differently scaled drift terms by the unweighted score of q_t f_t. It neither states the necessary ratio conditions nor derives the claimed verifier exponent lambda. Consequently, the asserted equivalence to sampling from p_0 f^lambda does not follow.

The proof additionally assumes the existence of a scalar annealed verifier whose gradient equals a covariance- or preconditioner-scaled verifier gradient. A general matrix-scaled gradient field need not be conservative, so this existence claim requires assumptions that are not provided. These are substantive problems with the main theoretical novelty.

Much of the algorithmic contribution is a reframing or modest variation of prior methods: local search is implemented through the existing TFG recurrence framework, BFS resampling is closely related to sequential Monte Carlo/Feynman-Kac steering, and DFS is a heuristic restart strategy. Direct controlled comparisons against TFG, SMC/Feynman-Kac steering, restart sampling, and the closely related diffusion inference-time search work are missing.

The image evidence is too narrow and potentially verifier-coupled for the broad claims. ImageNet evaluation covers only two classes with 256 samples per class, making FID unstable and unrepresentative; absolute FIDs are also poor. CompBench search and evaluation appear to use the same oracle models, without an independent evaluator or human study to reveal verifier overoptimization. Image and maze results lack repeated-run uncertainty.

Compute fairness and tuning costs are insufficiently documented. Temperatures, thresholds, evaluation times, backtracking depths, and guidance strengths are tuned by setting, but tuning costs and selection protocols are not adequately reported. Neural-function evaluations also do not reflect differing verifier, backpropagation, memory, and batching costs; wall-clock comparisons are absent.

The decision-making evaluation remains limited. Maze experiments use one start-goal task per environment, roughly 40 samples, and a verifier that does not detect collisions between consecutive waypoints. Offline RL employs separately tuned hyperparameters for every task, achieves an average slightly below QGPO, copies baseline results from prior work, and lacks a compute-matched ablation separating local guidance from Best-of-N selection. Overall, the promising empirical trends do not compensate for the unsupported central theorem and incomplete baseline isolation.

strengths: The paper presents a clear and useful unifying perspective: inference-time control of diffusion models as a combination of gradient-based local search and tree-based global search.

The proposed BFS-resampling, BFS-pruning, and DFS formulations are intuitive, broadly applicable, and include practically useful mechanisms such as intermediate verification, backtracking, and adaptive compute allocation.
The empirical scope is unusually broad, covering long-horizon planning, offline reinforcement learning, compositional text-to-image generation, and ImageNet conditional generation.

Results are consistently promising: search substantially improves maze success, achieves competitive D4RL scores without retraining the policy, and generally improves quality-versus-compute curves over best-of-N sampling.
The paper is well organized and supplies pseudocode, implementation choices, hyperparameters, and separate hyperparameter-search and evaluation seeds for the offline-RL experiments.
weaknesses: Proposition 1 is not established as rigorously as claimed. The derivation suppresses the relative scaling of the score, guidance, and noise terms when identifying the limiting Langevin SDE; it also asserts the existence of annealed verifier potentials without fully addressing integrability. Consequently, the claimed target distribution p0(x)f(x)^lambda and its lambda are not clearly derived for the general guidance configuration.

The theoretical result is an asymptotic continuous-step equivalence, whereas the experiments use few finite recurrence and denoising steps. No finite-discretization analysis or empirical validation of convergence to the claimed composed distribution is provided.

The image evaluation is too limited for the broad claims. ImageNet experiments use only two classes and 256 samples per class, making class-conditional FID noisy and unrepresentative; the reported FIDs are also quite high.

The CompBench verifier appears to serve both as the search objective and principal evaluation signal. Without independent evaluators or human assessment, improvements may partly reflect direct optimization of the metric rather than better compositional generation.

Compute comparisons use diffusion-model NFE but do not clearly incorporate verifier inference, verifier-gradient backpropagation, differing particle parallelism, or hyperparameter-search cost. This weakens the conclusion that the methods are universally more compute-efficient.

Several important ablations and baselines are missing, including direct comparisons against the underlying recurrent training-free-guidance algorithm, controlled local-only versus global-only comparisons across domains, sensitivity to imperfect or miscalibrated verifiers, and sensitivity to BFS/DFS schedules and thresholds.

The offline-RL method requires extensive task-specific hyperparameter tuning and a learned Q-function, while its average score is slightly below the strongest reported baseline. Thus, its practical training-free advantage is promising but not decisively demonstrated.

BFS resampling uses independent rounding of child counts, which need not preserve the stated particle budget; the paper does not explain budget correction or quantify its effect. Overall, the contribution is promising and close to acceptance, but the central theoretical and evaluation claims need stronger support.

The BFS study usefully organizes prior methods along interpretable tempering, scoring, and resampling choices; the SSP-based variant consistently improves the reported verifier score across two diffusion models and compute budgets.
Adaptive DFS is simple and practically appealing: its verifier threshold provides an understandable mechanism for allocating more computation to difficult instances.

The experiments cover several domains, including image generation, trajectory planning, offline RL, and policy distillation. The paper also recognizes reward hacking and tests a two-verifier mitigation.
The presentation is generally clear, with pseudocode, implementation details, compute accounting in NFEs, several ablations, and explicit comparisons to recent methods.
weaknesses: The theoretical claims are substantially stronger than the analysis supports. The claimed asymptotic exactness requires an appropriate annealing path and correctly calibrated guidance exponent, but the practical path is constructed from the biased approximation f(E[x0|xt]) and the paper does not show that its finite-step algorithm samples the distribution in Eq. 5. Reinterpreting recurrence as an approximate ULA update is not sufficient to establish exact sampling.

Theorem 1 relies on bounded-support, strongly log-concave, smooth targets, despite the motivating diffusion distributions being complex and multimodal. Some proof steps are only informal big-O assertions, and the resulting bound contains a nonvanishing finite-iteration term. It therefore offers little support for the paper's practical or multimodal setting.

Much of the empirical image evidence is measured with the same verifier used for search. The BFS experiments optimize and report ImageReward, while the DFS study similarly emphasizes verifier-derived scores. Independent human judgments or robust held-out perceptual metrics are missing, leaving reward overfitting as a major confound.

Evidence for the central joint local/global scaling claim is narrow. The principal Pareto study uses one custom PointMaze layout and one start-goal task with only roughly 40 samples per point. Offline RL uses Best-of-N rather than the proposed BFS/DFS, and the image experiments do not convincingly evaluate joint scaling.

Several evaluations are insufficiently reliable: class-conditional FID is computed from only 256 samples without uncertainty; MSP is a weak proxy for being in-distribution; many image and planning plots lack comprehensive statistical testing; and the claimed 2x efficiency advantages are not supported by wall-clock or memory measurements.

Novelty is fragmented and partly incremental: the improved BFS largely recombines known tempering, scoring, and resampling choices; DFS is threshold-triggered noising/backtracking; and local search is implemented through the existing TFG recurrence framework. The classical-search framing is intuitive, but does not by itself establish a sufficiently new algorithmic foundation.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite substantial appendix detail: the project-page URL is blank, code is not provided, some dataset sizes and evaluation definitions are unclear, and extensive per-task hyperparameter search makes it difficult to assess robustness or total selection cost. Overall, the broad claims of a principled new Pareto frontier are not supported strongly enough for a top-tier acceptance.

strengths: The paper studies an important problem and presents a broad framework spanning particle search, adaptive backtracking, gradient-based refinement, planning, offline RL, and image generation.

The BFS section usefully organizes several existing methods through common tempering, scoring, and resampling choices. The ablations indicate that variance-reduced SSP resampling and the proposed configuration improve over the reproduced alternatives.
The threshold-based search provides an intuitive mechanism for allocating more computation to apparently difficult instances, and the paper reports generally favorable compute-performance curves.
The appendices provide pseudocode, implementation details, hyperparameter tables, and an effort to theoretically connect recurrent guidance with Langevin dynamics.
weaknesses: The central theoretical claims are not adequately established. The claimed equivalence to Langevin MCMC relies on a continuous-step limit, whereas the experiments use coarse finite discretizations. More seriously, the argument that the mean-guidance vector field necessarily corresponds to the gradient of some scalar annealed verifier is asserted without sufficient conditions; a matrix-scaled gradient is not generally conservative. The required relation between guidance coefficients and the claimed terminal distribution p0(x)f(x)^lambda is also not derived.

Theorem 1 does not constitute a convincing convergence guarantee. Its proof suppresses essential dependence on dimension, smoothness/convexity constants, initialization, and step-size restrictions; replaces standard ULA contraction terms with an unsupported O(a+(1-a)^N) expression; and combines bounded support with unconstrained Langevin updates without specifying boundary handling. Consequently, describing the method as asymptotically exact or theoretically grounded is too strong.

Much of the algorithmic novelty is incremental. The BFS method combines design choices already present in prior SMC approaches, while the so-called DFS is a threshold-triggered restart/re-noising procedure without a conventional DFS stack or explicit sibling traversal. Local search is implemented through the existing TFG recurrence framework, and combining independently known local and global procedures is natural but not, by itself, a major technical advance.

Several evaluations optimize and report essentially the same verifier signal. The text-to-image BFS study relies on ImageReward, while the DFS study uses a VLM for both search and evaluation. There is no human evaluation or sufficiently independent held-out metric, making it difficult to distinguish genuine quality gains from verifier optimization. The DFS difficulty analysis is also partly tautological because difficulty and backtracking are both determined by closely related verifier scores.

Compute comparisons are incomplete: NFEs omit verifier evaluation, gradient/backpropagation, memory, and wall-clock costs, even though these can differ substantially across BoN, BFS, DFS, and local guidance. Statements such as “2x less computational cost” therefore do not establish overall efficiency.

The decision-making evidence is uneven. PointMaze uses only one custom maze/task with slightly more than 40 samples per point and incomplete uncertainty/reporting. Offline-RL gains are modest on average, involve extensive environment-specific hyperparameter selection, and compare against many numbers copied from prior work. The policy-distillation comparison to an online RL method is not controlled for data, interaction budget, tuning, or evaluation protocol.

The ImageNet reward-hacking experiment reports FID using only 256 samples, far below the sample count normally needed for a reliable FID estimate, and gives no confidence intervals. Maximum softmax probability is a weak and potentially miscalibrated proxy for being in-distribution. The results therefore do not substantiate the broad robustness claim.

Reproducibility remains limited despite the appendices: the project-page link is blank, code is not supplied, several exact search and guidance settings are missing, prompt/sample counts are unclear, and some reported “best” results arise from broad sweeps without a fully specified validation protocol.

The presentation repeatedly overstates conclusions—for example, that global search cannot exceed the base model, that the method establishes a new Pareto frontier broadly across decision-making domains, and that recurrence provides exact compositional sampling—relative to the limited benchmarks and assumptions. The limitations section does not discuss verifier bias, reward hacking beyond the small proposed test, theoretical restrictions, or the substantial inference cost.

strengths: The paper offers a timely and conceptually coherent framework that organizes diffusion inference-time scaling into complementary global and local search. The connection to classical BFS/DFS makes the design space intuitive and potentially useful to practitioners.

The adaptive DFS mechanism is an interesting contribution: verifier-triggered backtracking provides an explicit quality-compute control and empirically improves the Pareto frontier over Best-of-N and the authors' strengthened BFS baseline.

The BFS study usefully unifies several recent particle/tree-search approaches and isolates the effects of tempering, scoring, and resampling. The resulting Increase-Max-SSP configuration performs consistently well across two diffusion backbones and two particle budgets.

The empirical scope is unusually broad, covering text-to-image generation, long-horizon planning, offline reinforcement learning, policy distillation, and verifier reward hacking. Comparisons include strong and relevant baselines such as DAS, TFG, QGPO, and Diffusion-QL.

The paper explicitly recognizes verifier exploitation and proposes a simple double-verifier mitigation. The substantial improvements in FID, independent-classifier accuracy, and MSP are encouraging, even though the experiment is currently small.

The presentation is generally clear, with pseudocode, implementation details, hyperparameter ranges, and compute accounting in NFEs. Separating hyperparameter-search and evaluation seeds in the offline-RL experiments is good practice.
weaknesses: The theoretical claims are stronger than the derivation supports. In particular, the constructed annealed target has verifier exponent c_t/(a_t r_t), but the paper does not establish that the implemented schedules yield the claimed endpoint p_0(x)f(x)^lambda. The assertion that a potential function for the mean-guidance vector field necessarily exists also requires integrability conditions that are not stated.

The convergence theorem relies on restrictive assumptions that poorly match diffusion distributions and neural verifiers, and its bound suppresses important dependencies on initialization, dimension, strong-convexity and smoothness constants. Consequently, descriptions such as 'asymptotically exact' should be qualified, especially with an approximate learned score, posterior-mean verifier surrogate, finite-step ULA, and hyperparameter-tuned guidance.

Several evaluations optimize and report essentially the same verifier signal. This makes the image results vulnerable to verifier overfitting and weakens claims about perceptual quality. Independent evaluators or human judgments are needed for the BFS/DFS text-to-image experiments, not only for the separate reward-hacking study.

Statistical validation is uneven. The BFS gains over the strongest baselines are often modest without significance tests; the planning curves lack uncertainty estimates; and the double-verifier experiment computes FID from only 256 samples, which is too small for a stable FID comparison. The latter needs substantially more samples, multiple seeds, and clearer reporting of the evaluated classes.

The decision-making evidence is narrower than the framing suggests. PointMaze uses one custom layout and one start-goal task with a privileged ground-truth map verifier, while the offline-RL average is comparable to, rather than better than, QGPO. More environments, held-out maze layouts/tasks, and sensitivity analyses would strengthen the generality claim.

Some adaptivity evidence is partly mechanical: because DFS backtracks whenever its score falls below a threshold, showing that low-scoring prompts consume more compute does not by itself demonstrate better instance-wise allocation. A fixed-compute oracle, randomized control, or difficulty-stratified quality-compute comparison would make this claim more convincing.

Reproducibility remains incomplete for a method with many schedules and thresholds: key selection procedures and robustness across hyperparameters are not consistently reported, and the manuscript's project-page link is blank. The limitations section also understates verifier dependence, reward hacking, computational cost, and the restrictive theoretical assumptions.
